# Slack vs Element (2026)

## Overview
Slack and Element are communication platforms designed for teams and organizations. This comparison is aimed at teams considering a switch from Slack to Element, likely due to concerns about data ownership, cost, or specific feature requirements. The core use case for both tools is team collaboration, and the key reason someone would switch is to gain more control over their data and reduce costs.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Element is free and self-hosted, while Slack has a per-user monthly fee.
* Data ownership: Element allows teams to host their own servers, giving them full control over their data, while Slack stores data on its own servers.
* Setup complexity: Slack has a simpler setup process, while Element requires more technical expertise to self-host.
* Scalability: Slack is designed to scale with large teams, while Element's scalability depends on the team's self-hosting capabilities.
* Feature difference: Element has end-to-end encryption for all conversations, while Slack only offers this feature for certain paid plans.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Slack | Element |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $7.25-$15/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | Apache 2.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $362.50-$750/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1450-$3000/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
### Slack
* Easy to set up and use
* Large user base and community
* Integrates with many third-party apps
* Offers a free plan with limited features
* Scalable for large teams
### Element
* Free and self-hosted
* End-to-end encryption for all conversations
* Customizable and extensible
* Gives teams full control over their data
* Limited user base and community compared to Slack

## When to Choose Each
Slack is a good choice for teams that prioritize ease of use and scalability, and are willing to pay for these features. It's ideal for large teams with simple communication needs. Element, on the other hand, is a good choice for teams that require full control over their data and are comfortable with self-hosting. It's ideal for teams with high security requirements or those who want to avoid vendor lock-in.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Slack data using the Slack export tool, which provides a JSON file containing your team's conversations and other data.
2. Set up an Element server and configure it to your team's needs.
3. Use the Element import tool to import your Slack data into your new Element server.
4. Update your team's clients and settings to point to the new Element server.

## Our Take
Element is not yet production-ready for most users, as it requires technical expertise to set up and manage. One specific technical limitation worth knowing before switching is that Element's scalability depends on the team's self-hosting capabilities, which can be a challenge for large teams. However, for teams that require full control over their data and are comfortable with self-hosting, Element is a good choice. We recommend switching to Element if you're a small to medium-sized team with high security requirements and are willing to invest time in setting up and managing your own server.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams (less than 20 users) with high security requirements
* Teams that require full control over their data and are comfortable with self-hosting
* Teams that don't need Slack's advanced features and integrations
* Teams with limited budgets and want to avoid per-user fees
* Teams with experienced IT staff who can manage an Element server

## FAQ
### Can I use Element for free?
Yes, Element is free and self-hosted, which means you can use it without paying any per-user fees. However, you'll need to cover the costs of hosting your own server.
### Is Element as easy to use as Slack?
No, Element requires more technical expertise to set up and manage, especially for self-hosting. However, once set up, the user interface is similar to Slack and easy to use.
### Can I migrate my Slack data to Element?
Yes, you can export your Slack data using the Slack export tool and import it into Element using the Element import tool.
### Does Element have the same features as Slack?
No, Element has a more limited set of features compared to Slack, but it offers end-to-end encryption for all conversations and gives teams full control over their data.
### Is Element suitable for large teams?
Not yet, as Element's scalability depends on the team's self-hosting capabilities, which can be a challenge for large teams.

* Data ownership: Mattermost allows teams to host their own servers, giving them full control over their data, while Slack stores data on its own servers.

| Aspect | Slack | Mattermost |

* Easy to set up and use
* Wide range of integrations with third-party apps
* Good mobile app support
* Strong customer support

### Mattermost
* Self-hosted option gives teams full control over data
* Highly customizable and extensible
* Native integration with GitHub

* Teams that don't need Notion's comprehensive set of features
* Teams that are comfortable with self-hosting and have some technical expertise
* Solo users or freelancers who want a free and open-source alternative to Notion

## FAQ
### Can I use Logseq for large teams?
No, Logseq is not designed for large teams and may not be scalable for teams with more than 50 users.
### Is Logseq free?
Yes, Logseq is free and open-source, with no costs per user.
### Can I self-host Logseq?
Yes, Logseq allows self-hosting, giving you full control over your data.
### Does Logseq have a mobile app?
Not yet, but the Logseq team is working on a mobile app.
### Can I import my Notion data into Logseq?
Yes, Logseq has an import tool that supports importing data from Notion.

title: GitHub vs GitLab
comparison_markdown:
# GitHub vs GitLab

## Overview

GitHub is the world largest code hosting platform, owned by Microsoft, with 100 million developers. GitLab is a complete DevOps platform that can be fully self-hosted, offering everything from Git hosting to CI/CD and container registries.

## Key Differences

- **Cost**: GitHub free tier is generous; GitLab Community Edition is fully free to self-host
- **CI/CD**: GitLab has more powerful built-in CI/CD pipelines; GitHub Actions is catching up
- **Self-hosting**: GitLab is designed to be self-hosted; GitHub Enterprise self-hosted is expensive
- **Feature scope**: GitLab is a complete DevSecOps platform; GitHub focuses on developer collaboration
- **Community**: GitHub has a dramatically larger open-source community and project discoverability

## Pricing Comparison

| Aspect | GitHub | GitLab |
|--------|-------------------------------|-------------------------------|
| Base pricing | Free / $7-$21/user | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | MIT (CE) |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Cost at 50 users | See pricing page | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Cost at 200 users | See pricing page | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Vendor lock-in | High | None |

## Pros and Cons

### GitHub

**Pros:**
- Polished, professionally designed user interface
- Large ecosystem of official integrations
- Managed infrastructure with no server maintenance required
- Enterprise SLA and dedicated support available
- Mobile apps are well-maintained and reliable

**Cons:**
- Significant per-user monthly cost that scales linearly with team size
- Your data is stored on the vendor infrastructure
- No ability to inspect or modify the source code
- Feature roadmap controlled entirely by the vendor
- Risk of pricing changes, acquisition, or discontinuation

### GitLab

**Pros:**
- Free to self-host with costs only for server infrastructure
- Complete data ownership and privacy control
- Source code is auditable and modifiable
- Active open-source community
- No vendor lock-in or risk of sudden pricing changes
> GitHub: [gitlabhq/gitlabhq](https://github.com/gitlabhq/gitlabhq) * ~24k stars

**Cons:**
- Requires technical knowledge to self-host and maintain
- May lack some advanced features found in the proprietary version
- Support relies on community forums rather than a paid helpdesk
- UI polish may lag behind the proprietary tool
- You are responsible for updates, backups, and security patches

## When to Choose Each

**Choose GitHub if:** GitHub suits open-source projects wanting maximum community visibility or teams deeply integrated with GitHub Actions workflows.

**Choose GitLab if:** GitLab self-hosted is ideal for enterprises needing full control over their DevOps stack or regulated industries.

## Migration Path

GitLab provides a GitHub importer that migrates repositories, issues, PRs, wikis, and milestones. Update CI configuration from GitHub Actions to GitLab CI/CD YAML format.

## Our Take

GitLab is production-ready for most teams willing to invest a few hours in setup. The self-hosted version gives you identical or better functionality to the paid GitHub tiers, with no recurring per-seat cost.

The main technical limitation worth knowing: you are responsible for your own backups, updates, and uptime. If your server goes down, so does your GitLab instance. Plan for this with automated backups and a monitoring alert.

Our recommendation: if your team has at least one developer and you are paying more than $100/month for GitHub, switching to self-hosted GitLab will pay for itself within the first month. If nobody on your team is comfortable with Linux or Docker, stay on GitHub until you have that resource.

## Who Should Switch

- Startups under 20 people paying per-seat fees they cannot yet justify
- Dev teams who already self-host other tools and have the ops knowledge
- Organizations in jurisdictions with strict data residency requirements
- Teams who have evaluated GitHub paid features and only use the basics
- Founders and solopreneurs who want the functionality without the subscription

## FAQ

### Is GitLab free to use?
Yes. GitLab is free to self-host. Your only cost is the server, typically $6-$12/month on a VPS provider like DigitalOcean or Vultr.

### How hard is it to migrate from GitHub to GitLab?
For most teams, migration takes 2-4 hours. Export your GitHub data, follow the GitLab import guide, and test with a small group before switching everyone over.

### Does GitLab get regular updates?
Yes. GitLab has an active open-source community with regular releases. Check the GitHub repository for release frequency.

### Can I use GitLab without technical knowledge?
You need basic comfort with a VPS and command line. If that feels unfamiliar, there are managed hosting options that handle the server for you at a modest cost.

### What happens if GitLab development stops?
Because the source code is open, you can continue running whatever version you have indefinitely. You can also fork the project or switch to another tool at your own pace — no vendor can shut off your instance.

---
*Data sourced June 2026. Pricing and features change. Verify at [GitHub](https://github.com) and [GitLab](https://gitlab.com) before making decisions.*
meta_description: GitLab is a free, self-hosted alternative to GitHub. Compare pricing, features, and migration steps. See full comparison.

# GitHub vs Gitea (2026)

## Overview
GitHub and Gitea are two popular Git repository management tools used for version control and collaboration. This comparison is beneficial for developers, teams, and organizations looking to switch from a proprietary platform to a self-hosted, open-source solution. The core use case for both tools is to manage and track changes in code, with the key reason to switch being the desire for greater control over data and costs.

## Key Differences
* Cost: GitHub offers free and paid plans, while Gitea is free and self-hosted.
* Data ownership: GitHub stores data on its servers, whereas Gitea allows users to host their own data.
* Setup complexity: GitHub has a more straightforward setup process, while Gitea requires more technical expertise for self-hosting.
* Scalability: GitHub is designed for large-scale enterprises, while Gitea is better suited for smaller teams and organizations.
* Feature difference: GitHub offers integrated project management tools, whereas Gitea relies on external integrations for similar functionality.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | GitHub | Gitea |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | Free / $7-$21/user | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | MIT |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $350-$1050/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1400-$4200/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
**GitHub:**
* Large community and user base
* Integrated project management tools
* Easy setup and user interface
* Scalable for large enterprises
* Security features and support
**Gitea:**
* Free and self-hosted
* Open-source and customizable
* Lightweight and fast
* Simple and intuitive interface
* Limited scalability and support resources

## When to Choose Each
GitHub is suitable for large teams and enterprises that require integrated project management tools, high scalability, and robust security features. It is also a good choice for users who prioritize ease of use and a large community of developers. On the other hand, Gitea is ideal for small to medium-sized teams, individuals, and organizations that value data ownership, customization, and cost-effectiveness. It is also a good option for those who are comfortable with self-hosting and have the necessary technical expertise.

## Migration Path
1. Export your GitHub repository using the GitHub Export feature, which generates a ZIP archive of your repository.
2. Install Gitea on your server and configure the necessary settings.
3. Use the Gitea import tool to import your GitHub repository archive.
4. Update any external integrations or dependencies to point to your new Gitea instance.
5. Test your repository and ensure that all data and history have been successfully migrated.

## Our Take
Gitea is a production-ready alternative to GitHub for many users, offering a free and self-hosted solution with a simple and intuitive interface. However, one technical limitation worth noting is Gitea's limited scalability, which may not be suitable for very large teams or enterprises. For most users, Gitea is a viable option, but those who require integrated project management tools or high scalability may want to stick with GitHub.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams (less than 10 users) who do not need integrated project management tools
* Individuals who value data ownership and customization
* Organizations with limited budgets that cannot afford GitHub's paid plans
* Teams that require a self-hosted solution for security or compliance reasons
* Developers who prefer a lightweight and fast Git repository management tool

## FAQ
### Is Gitea free?
Yes, Gitea is free and open-source, with no costs or licensing fees.
### Can I self-host Gitea?
Yes, Gitea is designed for self-hosting, allowing users to host their own data and repositories.
### Does Gitea offer integrated project management tools?
No, Gitea relies on external integrations for project management functionality.
### Is Gitea suitable for large enterprises?
Not yet, as Gitea's scalability is limited compared to GitHub.
### Can I migrate my GitHub repository to Gitea?
Yes, Gitea offers an import tool that supports GitHub repository archives.

# Figma vs Penpot (2026)

## Overview
Figma and Penpot are two popular design and prototyping tools used by designers, developers, and product teams to create user interfaces, user experiences, and other visual designs. This comparison is beneficial for teams and individuals who are looking for a cost-effective, self-hosted, or open-source alternative to Figma. The core use case for both tools is collaborative design and prototyping, and someone would switch from Figma to Penpot for better data ownership, lower costs, or more flexibility.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Figma has a per-user pricing model, while Penpot is free and open-source.
* Data ownership: Penpot allows users to self-host and have full control over their design data, whereas Figma stores data on its servers.
* Setup complexity: Penpot requires more technical expertise to set up and self-host, whereas Figma is cloud-based and easy to sign up for.
* Scalability: Figma has better scalability and performance for large teams and complex designs, whereas Penpot may require more resources and optimization for large-scale use.
* Feature difference: Figma has a more extensive library of plugins and integrations, including popular tools like Slack and Trello, whereas Penpot has a smaller but growing ecosystem of integrations.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Figma | Penpot |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $12-$75/user/month | Free |
| License | Proprietary | MPL 2.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $600-$3750/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $2400-$15000/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
**Figma:**
* Pros:
	+ Easy to use and collaborate with team members
	+ Large library of plugins and integrations
	+ Scalable and performant for large teams and complex designs
	+ Well-established and reputable brand
	+ Good customer support
* Cons:
	+ Expensive, especially for large teams
	+ Limited control over design data
	+ No self-hosting option
**Penpot:**
* Pros:
	+ Free and open-source
	+ Self-hosting option for full control over design data
	+ Customizable and flexible
	+ Growing community of users and contributors
* Cons:
	+ Steeper learning curve due to technical requirements
	+ Limited library of plugins and integrations
	+ May require more resources and optimization for large-scale use
	+ Still in active development, with some features and stability issues
	+ Limited customer support

## When to Choose Each
Figma is a good choice for large teams, enterprises, or individuals who prioritize ease of use, scalability, and a wide range of integrations. It is also suitable for teams who are already invested in the Figma ecosystem and have a large library of designs and plugins. On the other hand, Penpot is a good choice for small to medium-sized teams, startups, or individuals who are looking for a cost-effective, self-hosted, or open-source alternative to Figma. It is also suitable for teams who value data ownership, customization, and flexibility.
Penpot is also a good choice for teams who are looking for a more transparent and community-driven development process. Figma, on the other hand, is a good choice for teams who are looking for a more established and reputable brand with good customer support.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Figma designs in SVG or PNG format.
2. Use the Penpot import tool to upload your designs to Penpot.
3. Configure your Penpot instance to match your Figma workflow, including setting up users, teams, and permissions.
4. Update your design files to take advantage of Penpot's features and capabilities.
5. Test and refine your designs in Penpot to ensure a smooth transition.

## Our Take
Penpot is still in active development, and while it shows promise, it may not be production-ready for most users right now. It lacks some of the features and polish of Figma, and its user interface can be overwhelming for new users. One specific technical limitation worth knowing before switching is that Penpot's performance can be affected by the size and complexity of your design files, so large teams or complex designs may require more resources and optimization. However, for small to medium-sized teams or individuals who value data ownership, customization, and flexibility, Penpot is definitely worth considering.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams (less than 10 users) who do not need advanced collaboration features
* Startups or individuals who are looking for a cost-effective alternative to Figma
* Teams who value data ownership and self-hosting
* Designers who are comfortable with technical requirements and customization
* Teams who do not need a wide range of integrations or plugins

## FAQ
### Can I use Penpot for free?
Yes, Penpot is free and open-source, and you can use it without paying any fees.
### Is Penpot self-hosted?
Yes, Penpot offers a self-hosting option, which allows you to have full control over your design data.
### Can I import my Figma designs into Penpot?
Yes, Penpot has an import tool that allows you to upload your Figma designs in SVG or PNG format.
### Is Penpot compatible with my operating system?
Penpot is a web-based application and can be accessed from any device with a modern web browser, regardless of the operating system.
### Can I use Penpot for large-scale designs?
While Penpot can handle complex designs, its performance may be affected by the size and complexity of your design files, so large teams or complex designs may require more resources and optimization.
